list.listitem: The American Urological Association (AUA) symptom score can accurately and reliably predict the severity of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). B
Prostate cancer should be considered in any patient with BPH symptoms. C
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists are equally effective and work rapidly; patients can expect moderate improvement in symptoms. A
5-Alpha reductase inhibitors modestly improve AUA symptom score and reduce the risk of acute urinary retention or need for invasive surgery. A

Combination therapy with an alpha blocker and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor is superior to monotherapy, particularly in patients with higher prostate volumes and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. B

background.definition: Lower urinary tract symptoms are commonly a result of bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). This is predominately due to two components: a static component related to an increase in benign prostatic tissue narrowing the urethral lumen and a dynamic component related to an increase in prostatic smooth muscle tone mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors.

list.listitem: The overall incidence rate is 15/1000 men/year.
Incidence increases linearly with age after age 50 years.
The overall prevalence rate of BPH is 10.3%. It increases linearly with age and affects 50% of the male population by age 50 and 80% by age 80.
In the United States approximately 14 million men suffer from BPH.
The annual cost of treatment is about $4 billion.

Systemic hormonal alterations with aging interact with growth factors to induce stromal or glandular hyperplasia of the prostate gland. For instance, men with hepatic cirrhosis are less likely to have BPH due to altered circulating levels of estrogens and androgens.

Heredity and racial factors may also play a role in causation. Men with family members who develop BPH under the age of 60 years are at a higher risk. Asian males are at lower risk for developing BPH than other groups in the United States.
Stromal and epithelial cell hyperplasia, predominantly in the transitional zone of the prostate: cells grow and form discrete adenomas causing bladder outlet obstruction.

Increased smooth muscle tone via stimulation of alpha-1-adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck, prostate, and prostate capsule: coupled with bladder dysfunction due to outflow obstruction and alterations in central nervous system input, cause the lower urinary tract symptoms of BPH.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Higher serum dihydrotestosterone (second to fourth quartiles)

list.listitem: The AUA symptom score and the International Prostate Symptom Score (I-PSS) can accurately and reliably predict the severity of BPH. B
Prostate cancer should be considered in any patient with BPH symptoms. C
A physical examination should be performed including a digital rectal examination and focused abdominal/neurologic examinations. C
A urinalysis should be performed to assess for hematuria or pyuria. C
Creatinine determination is no longer recommended as a routine measurement in patients with BPH. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Increased white count, abnormal urinary sediment, tender prostate gland
Low free PSA, increased PSA velocity greater than 0.75 ng/mL/y
Fever, abnormal urinary sediment, positive urine culture
Microscopic hematuria, abnormal cytology, bladder mass on imaging studies or cystoscopy
Increased residual volume after voiding; abnormal urodynamic studies

list.listitem: Obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, intermittency, weak stream, straining, and incomplete emptying. Irritative symptoms include urinary frequency, nocturia, and urgency.

However a recent systematic review concluded that typical signs and symptoms (hesitancy, poor urinary stream, straining, prolonged micturition, dribbling, frequency, urgency and nocturia) were minimally helpful in diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction when compared to the reference standard of pressure-flow studies performed by a urologist. Only the absence of nocturia (LR− 0.19) was possibly useful in ruling out bladder outlet obstruction.
The score of the self-administered AUA symptom test can reliably assess the severity of symptoms. Severity based on the AUA scores is as follows: mild 0 to 7, moderate 8 to 19, and severe 20 to 35.

A digital rectal examination should be done to estimate the size of the prostate. A focused abdominal/neurologic exam should be performed to consider other conditions that might contribute to voiding symptoms.

BPH is primarily a clinical diagnosis, and tests are not helpful in confirming the diagnosis; however, they are useful in ruling out other conditions with similar symptoms such as UTI, renal lithiasis, prostatitis, and bladder tumors.

In one study, intravesical prostatic protrusion and detrusor wall thickness on suprapubic ultrasound were significantly associated with bladder prostatic obstruction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.835 (95% CI 0.756-0.915) and 0.845 (95% CI 0.78-0.91), respectively).
Since obstructive uropathy is rare, measuring serum creatinine is not recommended.

Urinary tract imaging with ultrasound or CT are important in evaluating patients with BPH who also have recurrent UTI/hematuria, renal insufficiency, urolithiasis, or a prior history of urinary tract surgery.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and treatment of BPH. The AUA guideline can be found here.
Watchful waiting is an option; the need for medical treatment is based on symptoms (AUA symptom score) and the degree of patient bother. C
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists are equally effective and work rapidly; patients can expect moderate improvement in symptoms. A
5-alpha reductase inhibitors modestly improve the AUA symptom score and reduce the risk of acute urinary retention or need for invasive surgery. A
One year of phytotherapy (ie, saw palmetto) was no more effective than placebo in improving outcomes in patients with BPH. B
Combination therapy with an alpha blocker and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor is superior to monotherapy, particularly in patients with higher prostate volumes and PSA levels. B
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists are equally effective and improve symptoms and urine flow.
Alpha-adrenergic antagonist use is associated with a small risk of falling (OR 1.14) and sustaining a fracture (OR 1.16) compared to a nonexposed cohort, likley a result of induced hypotension.

Long-acting selective subtype (alpha-1A) alpha blockers such as tamsulosin and silodosin are prostate selective with minimal vascular effects which may be beneficial in patients at risk for orthostasis.
Use of alpha blockers increases the success rate of catheter removal following acute urinary retention but cost effectiveness, prevention of recurrence, and duration of treatment are unknown.

5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5aRIs), including finasteride and dutasteride, prevent acute urinary retention and surgery. You will need to treat about 100 men per year to prevent one from going into urinary retention and about 60 per year to avoid one surgery.
Dutasteride may reduce the risk of prostate cancer but increases risk of heart failure over placebo.

However a more recent study of 94,440 men with BPH failed to demonstrate that 5αRIs increased the risk of hospitalization for heart failure, myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death compared to non-use.
Long-term finasteride use, however, is also associated with an increase in the risk of high-grade prostate cancer.

Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors have been shown to demonstrate mild to modest improvement in symptom scores and peak flow rates in patients with BPH. This will also offer treatment of associated erectile dysfunction (ED) which may be associated with BPH.
Tadalafil has a modest effect on BPH symptoms similar to other alpha blockers.

Anticholinergics in combination with alpha blockers have been shown to improve symptom and bother scores in patients with BPH especially in patients with storage problems. The post-void volume should be monitored during therapy.

A systematic review of 12 studies with 4634 patients found minimal benefit with the addition of antimuscarinics to alpha-blockers for treating lower urinary tract symptoms in adults with BPH. Patients treated with antimuscarinics were at a higher risk of urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness. The antimuscarinics studied included oxybutynin, solifenacin, mirabegron, tolterodine, trospium, and vibegron, among others.

Combining alpha-adrenergic antagonists and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors slows BPH progression. You would have to treat 20 patients with combined therapy instead of monotherapy for 4 years to prevent one from having progressive symptoms. The benefit is greatest in patients with larger prostates and a PSA higher than 4 ng/mL.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been shown to improve flow measures and urinary symptoms in patients with BPH. Patients on NSAIDs should be monitored for esophageal reflux and peptic ulcer disease symptoms.
Naftopodil has been studied in several RCTs in Japan. None of the studies compared the drug to placebo; based on limited data, the drug may provide limited symptomatic benefits.

Desmopressin, an analogue of vasopressin, decreases symptoms of nocturia in adults. A dose of 100 mcg was associated with one additinoal hour of sleep prior to the first void, and 0.72 fewer episodes of nocturia per night compared to placebo. The most common adverse effects were hyponatremia and headache.

Patients likely to benefit from surgical therapy include those with very large prostates (volume over 80 g), those who have severe symptoms (AUA score greater than 20), those with acute urinary retention who fail a trial without catheter, and men with renal insufficiency due to obstructive uropathy. The resistive index measured using transrectal ultrasound may be useful in predicting success of TURP.
Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is the gold standard.

Minimally invasive therapies, including transurethral microtherapy (TUMT) and holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP), can be performed on an outpatient basis with local anesthesia with less short-term complications than more invasive therapy. Photoselective vaporization is a moderately invasive therapy requiring anesthesia. These therapies improve symptom scores and flow rates more so than medical therapy. Limited data on the long-term efficacy, cost, and retreatment rates are available.
A randomized trial comparing TURP with thulium laser transurethral vaporesection in 410 men, and found few differences in outcomes or adverse events.
Prostatic artery emblism was compared with TURP in a small (n = 103) RCT, and was slightly less effective based on the urinary symptom score (-9.2 vs -10.7 point improvement).

In a 10-year follow-up study of 66 men with lower urinary tract symptoms suggestive of BPH (44% of the original patients), there were similar and durable improvements in symptoms, mortality and failure rates among patients randomized to TURP, contact laser prostatectomy, and electrovaporization of the prostate.

A 3-year follow-up study comparing two laser techniques (photoselective vaporization and holmium laser ablation) for patients with BPH and small- to moderate-sized prostates reported comparable efficacy with improved quality of life (66% and 69%, respectively) and low re-treatment rates (19% and 16%, respectively).

In a systematic review of 10 moderate-poor quality trials, transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP) was equivalent to TURP in symptomatic improvement and had lower post-operative morbidity but higher risk of reoperation.

Small nonrandomized studies suggest short-term improvement in symptomatic BPH with the injection of ethanol, cetrorelix pamoate (a luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone receptor antagonist), or botulinum toxin into the prostate. However, additional studies are necessary to determine long-term efficacy and to assess safety concerns.
A Cochrane review identified 15 studies with 1585 patients, and concluded that while it was effective, TURP provided greater improvement in symptom scores.
Phytotherapy has been widely used by patients to improve BPH symptoms in the setting of mild to moderate disease but data are primarily from small, low-quality trials.

A Cochrane revew found that Serenoa repens (the presumed active ingredient of Saw Palmetto), used alone, shows minimal to no improvement in urinary tract symptoms or quality of life when compared to a placebo over three to six months. Additionally, this treatment probably does not cause adverse events. Similar outcomes were observed at 12 to 17 months.

This same review found that when combined with other herbal products, Serenoa repens may lead to little or no change in urinary tract symptoms. However, its effects on quality of life and the potential for adverse events are less certain.
However, a large, high-quality RCT using saw palmetto for 1 year demonstrated no difference in BPH outcomes compared with placebo.
A small RCT demonstrated improvement in lower urinary symptoms in men using cranberry powder.

Behavioral management such as limitation of fluids, bladder focused training, treatment of constipation, and review of the patient's medication list may impact symptoms of BPH and improve quality of life.
Botulinum toxin may be beneficial for selective patients with BPH.
Statins may reduced the incidence of BPH and the progression of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men over the age of 60.
Self-management options for men with lower urinary tract symptoms include education and reassurance, reduction of caffeine and alcohol intake, fluid management, and toilet and bladder training.
A systematic review identified 8 studies with 1006 adult men of self-management options and found clinically important benefits compared to usual care.
Most patients with BPH will require ongoing therapy.
Some patients may be able to discontinue alpha-adrenergic antagonists after several months of treatment.

Refer patients to a urologist if they have suspected prostate cancer, recurrent hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, acute urinary retention with failure of a trial without catheter, and increasing BPH symptoms refractory to medical therapy.
Approximately 20% of men will have BPH progression over a 5-year period. These patients typically have higher prostate volumes greater than 40 g and PSA levels greater than 1.4 ng/mL at baseline.

Approximately 2.5% of men with BPH will develop acute urinary retention after 5 years. These patients can initially be managed with an indwelling catheter and an alpha-adrenergic antagonist. Patients who fail a trial without catheter should be referred to a urologist.

A Cochrane review concluded that silver alloy indwelling catheters for hospitalized adults in the short-term reduced the risk of catheter-acquired UTI but cost-effectiveness is unclear; catheters impregnated with antibiotics are also beneficial in reducing bacteriuria in hospitalized adults catheterized for <1 week but data are inconclusive about those catheterized for longer periods.
Men rarely develop UTIs secondary to BPH. However, when this occurs patients can be treated with antibiotics in a standard fashion.
Because it is a rare complication of BPH, other etiologies for renal insufficiency should be suspected in patients with BPH who develop renal insufficiency.
Sexual dysfunction may be associated with BPH or result from medical or surgical therapy. Treatment with PDE-5 therapy may be beneficial in patients with associated ED and BPH.

Among men with prostatectomy followed for up to 12 months, it is not known which, if any, conservative treatments work for post-surgery urinary incontinence. A recent Cochrane review noted conflicting evidence for pelvic floor muscle training (with or without biofeedback), electrical stimulation and external magnetic innervation, or combinations of therapies.
Overactive bladder may be associated with BPH. Treatment with alpha blockers and anticholinergics may benefit these patients symptomatically.

A 2017 Cochrane Review concluded that in spite of 31 RCTs studying intermittent bladder catheterizations for long-term bladder management, there exists no convincing evidence that the incidence of urinary tract infections is affected by technique (aseptic or clean), the use of coated or uncoated catheters, sterile or clean catheters or self- vs other catheterizations.

Approximately 25% to 30% of patients with moderate to severe BPH will have worsening symptoms after 4 to 5 years. Patients at higher risk for progression include those with higher baseline prostate volumes (>40 g) and PSA levels (>1.4 ng/mL). B
Approximately 2.5% of patients on placebo develop acute urinary retention, and 6% develop symptoms warranting surgery. B
The AUA symptom score, I-PSS and PSA can also be used to document improvement or worsening of patients' symptoms. B
BPH increases with age. Nearly 80% of men over the age of 70 years have lower urinary tract symptoms. Lower urinary tract symptoms have been closely associated with sexual dysfunction in older men.
